title.narrative: Number of government policies developed or revised with civil society organization participation through EU support

description.narrative: This indicator refers to the number of government policies and strategies developed with Civil Society Organisation (CSO) participation through EU support. Components: CSO: Includes all nonState, notforprofit structures, nonpartisan and nonviolent, through which people organise to pursue shared objectives and ideals, whether political, cultural, social or economic. Operating from the local to the national, regional and international levels, they comprise urban and rural, formal and informal organisations. Participation: A process through which the government actively seeks the opinions of CSOs (interested and affected groups) for a policy initiative. Public participation process comprises the following characteristics: oIt is an integral part of the policy making system, meaning that it is not something spontaneous, or a decision made on the spot by public institutions but is included in the routine processes of the institution, oThe goal of public participation is better public policy, in the sense of more responsive policies to real citizen needs and with a higher degree of public support,oParticipants have a certain degree of influence on the final decisionPolicies: Includes government programmes, strategies and legislation. At central level developed/revised policies are counted for this indicator once they are endorsed by the Government. At the local level developed/revised policies are counted for this indicator once they are endorsed by the relevant authorities.

title.narrative: Total amount of waste generated in partner LGUs per year

description.narrative: This indicator will track reduction of wastes generated, which will improve circularity, and reduce wastes that are sent to landfills, thus prolonging the life of these waste facilities. The total amount of waste generated includes both hazardous and nonhazardous wastes in partner LGUs during the year. Components:Waste: Includes any nonhazardous or hazardous material that is discarded and managed at recycling facilities or disposal sites. More specifically, solid waste refers to recyclables, organic materials (such as food waste) and garbage generated by residential sources (households) and nonresidential sources, which include households, commerce and trade, small businesses, office buildings, and institutions (schools, hospitals, government buildings). It also includes waste from selected municipal services, e.g., waste from park and garden maintenance, waste from street cleaning services (street sweepings, the content of litter containers, market cleansing waste), if managed as waste. Electronic waste, or ewaste, refers to all items of electrical and electronic equipment and its parts that have been discarded as waste without the intent of reuse.

title.narrative: % of variation in attitudes and behaviours of targeted stakeholders around circular economy principles and practices

description.narrative: This indicator measures the percentage change of a target audience reporting that they hold a particular attitude or have engaged in a particular related to CE. It is assumed that the targeted audience has received messages related to CE principles and practices and as a result, the percentage of the audience with the desired attitudes and behaviours changes.Components:Target audience: The population whose attitude and/or behaviour related CE the intervention seeks to change. The target audience needs to be explicitly defined, including the LGU in which it occurs and the demographic segment it represents within the broader population.Attitude: Beliefs and feelings about CE principles and practices. Attitude can influence how individuals respond to various situations and can be positive, negative, or neutral, which may be expressed by statements such as I agree that recycling benefits the environment in my community.Behaviour: Actions undertaken by members of the target audience that result in more responsible consumption and production, which may be reported by statements such as, In the past month, I have sorted my household waste into garbage, recycling, and compost for pickup by the city.

title.narrative: Number of government policies developed or revised with civil society organization participation through EU support

description.narrative: This indicator refers to the number of government policies and strategies developed with Civil Society Organisation (CSO) participation through EU support. Components: CSO: Includes all nonState, notforprofit structures, nonpartisan and nonviolent, through which people organise to pursue shared objectives and ideals, whether political, cultural, social or economic. Operating from the local to the national, regional and international levels, they comprise urban and rural, formal and informal organisations. Participation: A process through which the government actively seeks the opinions of CSOs (interested and affected groups) for a policy initiative. Public participation process comprises the following characteristics: oIt is an integral part of the policy making system, meaning that it is not something spontaneous, or a decision made on the spot by public institutions but is included in the routine processes of the institution, oThe goal of public participation is better public policy, in the sense of more responsive policies to real citizen needs and with a higher degree of public support,oParticipants have a certain degree of influence on the final decisionPolicies: Includes government programmes, strategies and legislation. At central level developed/revised policies are counted for this indicator once they are endorsed by the Government. At the local level developed/revised policies are counted for this indicator once they are endorsed by the relevant authorities.

title.narrative: Total amount of waste generated in partner LGUs per year

description.narrative: This indicator will track reduction of wastes generated, which will improve circularity, and reduce wastes that are sent to landfills, thus prolonging the life of these waste facilities. The total amount of waste generated includes both hazardous and nonhazardous wastes in partner LGUs during the year. Components:Waste: Includes any nonhazardous or hazardous material that is discarded and managed at recycling facilities or disposal sites. More specifically, solid waste refers to recyclables, organic materials (such as food waste) and garbage generated by residential sources (households) and nonresidential sources, which include households, commerce and trade, small businesses, office buildings, and institutions (schools, hospitals, government buildings). It also includes waste from selected municipal services, e.g., waste from park and garden maintenance, waste from street cleaning services (street sweepings, the content of litter containers, market cleansing waste), if managed as waste. Electronic waste, or ewaste, refers to all items of electrical and electronic equipment and its parts that have been discarded as waste without the intent of reuse.

title.narrative: Number of people, staff of the LGUs and/or other local stakeholders, who have improved their knowledge on financing strategies, budget management and publicprivate partnerships for the implementation of CE initiatives

description.narrative: This indicator measures the increase in knowledge among LGU staff and local stakeholders regarding financing strategies, budget management, and publicprivate partnerships essential for implementing Circular Economy (CE) initiatives. The indicator tracks educational and training outcomes that enhance participants understanding and skills in these areas.Components:Knowledge Increase: This refers to the enhancement of understanding or skills in specific areas, in this case, financing strategies, budget management, and publicprivate partnerships (PPPs). It implies an educational or training component where participants gain new insights or competencies.Financing Strategies and Budget Management: These are crucial for the effective planning and execution of projects, particularly in the context of circular economy initiatives. This includes understanding how to allocate resources efficiently and manage financial risks associated with such projects.PublicPrivate Partnerships: PPPs are collaborations between public entities and private companies to finance, build, and operate projects that might otherwise be solely public sector tasks. Knowledge in this area would encompass understanding the structuring of these partnerships, the distribution of risks and rewards, and the regulatory and financial frameworks that govern such relationships.Circular Economy Initiatives: These initiatives focus on minimizing waste and making the most of resources. This involves strategies such as recycling, reusing, and extending the life cycle of products. Understanding the financial and managerial aspects of implementing these strategies at a local level is crucial for the effective adoption of circular economy principles.

title.narrative: Number of innovative finance instruments and investment strategies developed in coordination with the LGUs and the private stakeholders to support genderresponsive CE initiatives

description.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of innovative finance instruments (such as green bonds, gender bonds, sustainabilitylinked loans) and investment strategies (such as impact investing funds, ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) integrated portfolios) that have been developed and formally implemented in partnership with Local Government Units (LGUs) and private stakeholders. These financial instruments and strategies are specifically designed to fund and promote projects that incorporate genderresponsive approaches within circular economy initiatives.Components:Innovative Finance Instruments: These are nontraditional financial tools tailored to support sustainability, which might include green bonds, sustainabilitylinked loans, or equity funds that prioritize gender equality and environmental impact in their investment criteria.Investment Strategies: Plans or approaches adopted by investors or fund managers that explicitly aim to support and scale up circular economy projects with a genderresponsive focus, ensuring that investments contribute to both environmental sustainability and gender equality.Coordination with LGUs and Private Stakeholders: This involves the collaborative efforts between local government units and private sector entities to design and implement the aforementioned financial instruments and strategies.Support for GenderResponsive CE Initiatives: This specifies that the instruments and strategies are aimed at circular economy projects that explicitly consider and aim to benefit women, ensuring inclusivity and addressing genderspecific needs and impacts.

description.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of distinct local authorities, civil society organizations (CSOs), and private stakeholders that are actively involved in Circular Economy (CE) multistakeholder platforms within targeted Local Government Units (LGUs). Involvement is defined as participating in at least one meeting or contributing to one decision or document.The Philippines, Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG,) defines a Civil Society Organization (CSO) as a nonstate and nonprofit association that works to improve society and the human condition. Basic types of CSOs include nongovernmental organizations, peoples organizations, civic organizations, cooperatives, social movements, professional groups, and business groups1. Components:Local Authorities: Includes any governmental or administrative bodies at the local level, such as city councils, municipal departments, or other local government agencies.CSOs: Refers to nongovernmental organizations, nonprofit organizations, community groups, advocacy groups, and other civil society entities engaged in the region.Private Stakeholders: Encompasses businesses, corporations, small and mediumsized enterprises (SMEs), industry associations, and other private sector participants involved in circular economy practices.CE Multistakeholder Platforms: These are collaborative entities or committees that bring together various stakeholders to discuss, plan, and implement circular economy initiatives. They are typically characterized by regular meetings, shared goals or projects, and joint activities aimed at promoting sustainable resource use and waste reduction.Targeted LGUs: Specifies the local government units where these multistakeholder platforms are active, focusing on those specifically targeted by the project for circular economy enhancements.

description.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of distinct local authorities, civil society organizations (CSOs), and private stakeholders that are actively involved in Circular Economy (CE) multistakeholder platforms within targeted Local Government Units (LGUs). Basic types of CSOs include nongovernmental organizations, peoples organizations, civic organizations, cooperatives, social movements, professional groups, and business groups1. description.narrative: This indicator quantifies the number of Local Government Units (LGUs) that have improved their data management systems specifically for Circular Economy (CE) interventions and Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) tracking, with improvements including the disaggregation of data by Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GEDSI) factors. This encompasses upgrades to databases and Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting, and Learning (MERL) platforms to facilitate detailed, inclusive data analysis and reporting.Components:GEDSIDisaggregated: The databases and MERL platforms must be capable of reporting data that is disaggregated by gender and other social inclusion factors, enabling the analysis of impacts and participation across different demographic groups.CE Databases: Information systems that specifically track and manage data related to circular economy activities, including resource usage, waste management, recycling rates, and other relevant environmental sustainability metrics.MERL Platforms: Systems used for the ongoing monitoring, evaluation, and reporting of project activities, outcomes, and impacts, as well as for learning from these activities to inform future projects.Improvements: Enhancements made to existing systems that increase their capacity to collect, manage, analyze, and report disaggregated data. Improvements could include software upgrades, integration of new data collection methodologies, training of personnel on GEDSI aspects, or enhancements to data analysis capabilities.CE Interventions and NDC Contributions: Initiatives undertaken by LGUs to promote circular economy principles and practices, which also contribute to the fulfilment of the commitments made under their Nationally Determined Contributions for climate action.EUGEPP Support: Involvement by the EUGEPP in terms of funding, technical assistance, or capacitybuilding efforts that facilitate these improvements.

description.narrative: This indicator tracks the number of Local Government Units (LGUs) that have successfully developed Circular Economy (CE) strategies and portfolios that are responsive to Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GEDSI) principles. description.narrative: The ultimate objective of the Climate Change Convention (UNFCCC) is to achieve the stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system. Estimating the levels of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and removals is an important element of the efforts to achieve this objective. In accordance with Articles 4 and 12 of the Climate Change Convention and the relevant decisions of the Conference of the Parties, countries that are Parties to the Convention submit national GHG inventories to the Climate Change secretariat. These submissions are made in accordance with the reporting requirements adopted under the Convention, such as the revised Guidelines for the preparation of national communications by Parties included in Annex I to the Convention, Part I: UNFCCC reporting guidelines on annual greenhouse gas inventories (decision 24/CP.19) for Annex I Parties and Guidelines for the preparation of national communications for nonAnnex I Parties (decision 17/CP.8). The inventory data are provided in the annual GHG inventory submissions by Annex I Parties and in the national communications and biennial update reports by nonAnnex I Parties. The Paris Agreement adopted in 2015 marks the latest step in the evolution of the UN climate change regime and builds on the work undertaken under the Convention. Its central aim is to strengthen the global response to the threat of climate change by keeping a global temperature rise this century well below 2 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase even further to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The Agreement also aims to strengthen the ability of countries to deal with the impacts of climate change.Data reported against SDG indicators can be retrieved from the official UN SDG Database and Statistics https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/unsdg. Users are not expected to encode values for these indicators.For more information, see the SDG indicators metadata at https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/metadata/files/Metadata130202.pdf
